pronunciation.approximation: 'RAH-ee-jeen' — the 'r' is a light tap, and the final 'n' is a soft nasal.

kin.label: Pairing
kin.form: Fūjin, the wind god — born, like Raijin, from Izanagi's purification breath (Kojiki)

kin.label: Indian counterpart
kin.form: Indra, the Vedic thunderer, mediated through Buddhist Taishakuten

pronunciation.note: Raijin is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. He is the thunder god, often paired with Fūjin at temple gates; the script has no diacritic the ASCII form loses.

domains.title: God of Thunder and Lightning
domains.subtitle: Storms, Drums, and Temple Guardianship
domains.lead: Raijin is the thunder god of Japan, a fierce, demon-like kami who beats drums to create thunder and hurls lightning bolts. He is the counterpart of Fūjin, the wind god, and the two are often depicted together at the gates of Buddhist temples, where their terrifying forms ward off evil. Beneath the demon mask lives one of Japan's oldest powers: thunder, the voice of the dead world breaking into ours.

cards.name: Thunder Drummer
cards.desc: He beats drums set around his body to produce thunder; the number of rings on the drums counts the storm's strength.

cards.name: Lightning Hurling
cards.desc: He casts lightning in the shape of arrows or writhing thunder-snakes from the storm clouds.

cards.name: Fūjin's Companion
cards.desc: Paired with the wind god in temple art and architecture for more than a thousand years.

cards.name: Demon Guardian
cards.desc: His fierce form protects temples from harmful influences; as one of the Twelve Devas he guards the Dharma itself.

symbols.name: Thunder drums
symbols.meaning: The ring of drums around his body; each beat of thunder is a drumstroke, and the rings on the drumheads count them

symbols.name: Lightning bolts
symbols.meaning: The arrows or thunder-snakes (raiki) he casts from the clouds

symbols.name: Demon face
symbols.meaning: His fierce oni expression — the standard visual grammar of Japanese protective deities, whose ugliness is a shield

symbols.name: Storm clouds
symbols.meaning: The dark clouds from which he emerges, drawn as a floating island of thunder

mythology.lead: Raijin's mythology is a palimpsest: the thunder kami of the Kojiki, the Buddhist guardian of esoteric temple art, the storm god of the Mongol-invasion legend, and the bogey of nursery warnings — four layers of one drumbeat. The sources are layered and partly at odds, and each layer tells us what thunder meant to a different Japan.

myths.title: Thunder Born of the Dead Goddess
myths.text: In the Kojiki, Izanami dies from the burns of the fire god Kagutsuchi, and her grieving husband Izanagi pursues her into Yomi, the land of the dead. When he breaks his promise not to look, he sees her body corrupted; in her fury Izanami sends the yakusa no ikazuchi — the eight thunder spirits — in pursuit, together with the hags of Yomi. The text explains that these thunderers were born from the filth of Izanami's dying body. Izanagi escapes at the Even Pass of Yomotsu Hirasaka and seals the way with a boulder. Thunder, then, is older than the cleanly born gods: it issues from death itself, from the corruption of the beloved. Fūjin, by contrast, is born later, from Izanagi's breath during his river purification — wind as the breath of the purified, thunder as the voice of the dead. The later Buddhist painters gave this archaic terror his demon drums and his cloud-island, but the Kojiki keeps the older truth: the storm speaks with the voice of the world we have lost.

myths.title: Guardian of the Dharma
myths.text: With the arrival of esoteric Buddhism, the thunder power was enrolled in the defenses of the Dharma. From the Heian period, Raijin appears among the Jūni-ten, the Twelve Devas who guard the four directions and the zenith and nadir of the mandala, and with Fūjin he comes to stand at temple gatehouses — the pair most famously at the great Nioh-mon gates of Zen temples, where their sculpted forms confront visitors with the storm itself. His drumbeats scatter demons; his lightning burns away obstacles; his ugliness is itself a weapon, since in Buddhist iconography the fierce faces (the same grammar as the Nioh guardians) are shields that frighten evil before it can enter. Native kami and Buddhist guardian are not rivals here but one figure read twice: the Kojiki's thunderer and the mandala's defender are the same sound heard through two theologies. Japan's thunder god guards the gate because thunder has always guarded the boundary between worlds.

myths.title: Raijin and the Mongol Storms
myths.text: In 1274 and again in 1281, typhoons destroyed the invasion fleets Kublai Khan sent against Japan. The warrior Takezaki Suenaga, who fought in both campaigns, commissioned the picture-scroll Mōko Shūrai Ekotoba (c. 1293), whose final scenes show the fleet shattered and drowning in the tempest. Medieval chronicles credited the court's prayers to Hachiman and Amaterasu, but in the popular imagination the storms were the direct work of the storm gods — Raijin drumming the clouds open above the strait while Fūjin filled them with wind. Later tradition named the typhoons kamikaze, the 'divine wind'. The legend grew into one of Japan's foundational stories of being saved by the gods, invoked again in the twentieth century — for catastrophic ends — as proof that the islands enjoyed supernatural protection. Whatever the theology, the myth records a real memory: that the sea between Japan and the continent belongs to the storm gods, and that they have defended it before.

myths.title: Thunder and the Navel
myths.text: Japanese folk belief holds that Raijin eats the navels of children. During thunderstorms, parents ordered children to cover their bellies — heso o kakusu — and the custom persists idiomatically today, where covering the navel is also said to prevent catching cold. Behind the bogey lies an older logic: the navel is the body's center and its first scar, the mark of the cut that began independent life, and in folk anatomy it is the belly that illness and hunger strike first. Lightning, the sky's predator, seeks the exposed center of life just as thunder frightens the body's center of courage. The belief turns Raijin into the most domestic of terrors — not a god of cosmic battles but the reason a child clutches a blanket in a storm. The thunder god lives in the nursery because that is where fear is taught, and where protection is first learned.

lore.syncretism: Raijin descends from Indian Indra through the Buddhist Taishakuten, but he is no simple borrowing: the Kojiki's thunder spirits born of Izanami's body are native and older, and the mature Raijin is the fusion of both lines. In esoteric Buddhism he serves among the Twelve Devas, and his permanent pairing with Fūjin expresses the Japanese reading of storms as coupled powers — wind and thunder — rather than as one god's attribute. The medieval kamikaze legend added a third layer, national salvation; the nursery warning a fourth, domestic discipline. Each tradition kept the same figure because each needed the same thing: a way to say that the storm is not random.
lore.culturalLegacy: Raijin remains one of Japan's most visually striking deities. His most famous portrait, Tawaraya Sōtatsu's Fūjin-Raijin-zu screens (early seventeenth century, now a National Treasure at Kennin-ji in Kyoto), is a canonical image of Japanese art, endlessly reproduced. The Kaminarimon — 'Thunder Gate' — of Sensō-ji in Asakusa has guarded the temple approach since 942, its great red lantern one of Tokyo's landmarks. He drums his way through ukiyo-e, manga, anime, and video games as the archetype of overwhelming natural power, and the old folk instruction to cover one's navel in a storm is still spoken to Japanese children. Few gods so terrifying in appearance live so comfortably in a modern city.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Raijin is the sound of the sky's anger and the light that splits the darkness. He reminds us that nature is not merely beautiful; it is also loud, dangerous, and alive. To stand before Raijin is to feel small before the storm — and Japan, sitting in the typhoon belt on the Pacific Ring of Fire, has more reason than most civilizations to keep that feeling close.

Yet the same tradition that made him a demon made him a guardian. The drum that terrifies the child also warns the temple; the lightning that burns the tree also marks the god who protects the gate. Raijin holds both truths without embarrassment. In an age that likes to separate danger from safety, he is the older, wiser figure: the same sky does both, and the wise household covers its navel and keeps its gate.

lore.archaeology: Raijin's material record is pictorial and architectural rather than inscriptional. The supreme witness is Tawaraya Sōtatsu's Fūjin-Raijin-zu (early seventeenth century, ink and color on paper, National Treasure, Kennin-ji, Kyoto), which fixed the modern image of the drum-ringed thunderer. The Kaminarimon ('Thunder Gate') of Sensō-ji, Asakusa, first built in 942 and rebuilt in 1960 after the 1865 fire, enshrines Fūjin and Raijin statues above its famous lantern. Sets of the Twelve Devas (Jūni-ten) at esoteric temples such as Tō-ji in Kyoto preserve Heian-period sculptural lineages of the thunder guardian, and Hokusai's manga sketches spread his likeness to every corner of Japan.
